headline: Designing Real-Time Voice Agents for responsive streaming audio conversations
summary: Achieving responsive voice agents requires careful coordination across audio capture, processing, and playback, managing partial turns and connection states for seamless interaction.
details: A voice agent feels responsive when it can process and return audio as a conversation unfolds. That requires coordination among audio capture, transport, model processing, playback, and conversational state. A model response alone is only one part of the experience.

To identify potential delays or failures, map out each stage from the user's microphone to returned audio: capture and buffering, connection setup, audio transmission, model processing, response streaming, and playback. This clarifies what the application controls versus what depends on network and provider behavior.

Streaming allows processing to begin before a complete recording is available. However, it also means the application must manage partial turns and connection state, rather than assuming each request is one finished file.

Key design decisions include how the system detects when a user finishes speaking, handles unclear speech, and manages interruptions. If interrupted, client and server need a consistent way to stop or replace current output to prevent stale audio from playing.

Testing should be conducted on expected devices and networks, as clean microphone recordings may not reveal problems from background noise, short pauses, packet loss, or mid-sentence changes. Distinguish listening, processing, speaking, and reconnecting states.

Define what the user hears when a connection drops, whether a turn can be safely retried, and how the system avoids responding twice to the same input. Treat any reported outcome as a specific result, not a verified benchmark or a guarantee for other deployments.

headline_marked: [[Five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5]] using GVS5H Harness for frontier coding
headline: Five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 using GVS5H Harness for frontier coding
summary: The new ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration method allows open-weight models to achieve 92.4% pass@1, approaching or exceeding proprietary models at a fraction of the cost.
details: A new training-free method, ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, enables fresh instances of one model to decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem.
This method yields significant gains, up to 25.6 percentage points, across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems.
Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reached 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% on LiveCodeBench, doing so at just 9% of the cost.
For locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B models, the accuracy rose from 66.8% to an impressive 92.4% pass@1.
This inference-time organization approach can achieve frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, and can even slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights.
However, the gains are not universal; some models showed no change or even worse performance when using this method.
Transcript analysis attributes the performance improvements primarily to effective problem decomposition and the use of persistent context during the orchestration process.
The code for this project is released under the MIT License, while the paper, figures, and run data are available under CC BY 4.0.
caption:
Open-weight Qwen3.8-27B models can now match proprietary frontier coding performance at a fraction of the cost.

A new training-free method, ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, enables fresh instances of one model to decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem.

This method yields significant gains, up to 25.6 percentage points, across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems.

Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reached 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% on LiveCodeBench, doing so at just 9% of the cost.

For locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B models, the accuracy rose from 66.8% to an impressive 92.4% pass@1.

This inference-time organization approach can achieve frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, and can even slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights.

However, the gains are not universal; some models showed no change or even worse performance when using this method.

Transcript analysis attributes the performance improvements primarily to effective problem decomposition and the use of persistent context during the orchestration process.

The code for this project is released under the MIT License, while the paper, figures, and run data are available under CC BY 4.0.
